modules.summary: Compare auto, home, health, life, disability, and liability coverage, then the commercial, government, and newer product lines.

sections.heading: Auto and home
paragraphs: Auto liability coverage pays others when the insured driver is at fault. Split limits such as 50/100/25 mean $50,000 per injured person, $100,000 total for injuries in one accident, and $25,000 for property damage. Each state sets minimum limits, and Maryland also requires personal injury protection and uninsured motorist coverage. Collision pays for damage to the insured car from a crash. Comprehensive pays for other causes such as theft, hail, fire, or hitting a deer. Uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage protects the insured when the at-fault driver lacks enough insurance.

Homeowners forms are named HO-1 through HO-8. The HO-3 is the most common policy for owner-occupied houses. The HO-4 is renters insurance, which covers belongings and liability but not the building. The HO-6 covers condominium owners. A homeowners policy has standard sections: Coverage A for the dwelling, B for other structures, C for personal property, D for loss of use, E for personal liability, and F for medical payments to others. Floods and earthquakes are usually excluded. Flood coverage is available through the National Flood Insurance Program and private insurers.

example.scenario: A driver with 50/100/25 limits causes a crash. One person has $70,000 of injuries, a second has $20,000, and the other car has $30,000 of damage.
example.solution: Bodily injury: the policy pays $50,000 for the first person (the per-person limit) and $20,000 for the second, totaling $70,000, under the $100,000 accident limit. Property damage: it pays $25,000, the limit. The driver is personally responsible for the remaining $20,000 of injury costs and $5,000 of property damage.

sections.heading: Health, life, and disability
paragraphs: A health deductible is the amount the insured pays before the plan shares costs. Coinsurance is the insured's percentage after the deductible. A copay is a flat fee for a service. The out-of-pocket maximum caps what the insured pays in a year for covered care. An HMO requires in-network care and usually a primary care referral. A PPO allows out-of-network care at higher cost.

Term life insurance covers a set period, has no cash value, and costs the least for young buyers. Whole life covers the insured's lifetime and builds cash value at a guaranteed rate. Universal life has flexible premiums and death benefits. Variable life invests cash value in subaccounts, so its value can fall. Disability insurance replaces part of income when illness or injury prevents work. The elimination period is the waiting time before benefits start.

Medicare is federal health insurance mainly for people 65 and older and some younger people with disabilities. Part A covers hospital care, Part B covers doctor and outpatient care, Part C (Medicare Advantage) is private plans that replace A and B, and Part D covers prescription drugs. Medicaid is a joint federal and state program based on financial need, and each state runs its own version.

example.scenario: A member has a $1,000 deductible, 20% coinsurance, and a $4,000 out-of-pocket maximum. A covered hospital bill is $3,000.
example.solution: The member pays the first $1,000, then 20% of the remaining $2,000, which is $400. The member's total is $1,400 and the plan pays $1,600. The member is still well under the $4,000 maximum.

sections.heading: Liability and commercial lines

rows: Liability above auto and home limits
Damage to business buildings, equipment, and inventory
Lost income while a covered loss closes the business
Injuries and property damage to others from business operations or premises
A package of property and liability coverage for small businesses
Claims against leaders for management decisions
Injuries caused by products the business makes or sells
Data breach response, ransomware, and related liability
Medical care and lost wages for work-related injuries, regardless of fault; required by state law
Losses from defects in a property's past ownership record; paid once at closing
Goods in transit and movable property
Guarantees that a party will fulfill a contract; the surety may seek repayment from that party

paragraphs: Unemployment insurance is a government program run by each state and funded mainly by employer payroll taxes. Disaster coverage combines several sources: property policies, flood and earthquake coverage, and federal assistance. International businesses buy political risk insurance and coverage for foreign operations. Farms use federal crop insurance through the USDA Risk Management Agency. Newer products include usage-based auto insurance that prices by measured driving, parametric insurance that pays a set amount when an event such as a wind speed occurs, and on-demand coverage bought for a single trip or item.

sections.heading: Match coverage to a need
paragraphs: Start with what could be lost: property, income, health, or the ability to pay a lawsuit. Then name the coverage that responds and the gaps that remain.

practice.task: A family rents an apartment, owns one car with a loan, has a new baby, and one parent runs a small online design business from home. List the coverage they should review and one gap for each.
practice.answer: Renters (HO-4) for belongings and liability; home business equipment may be excluded, so add a rider or BOP. Auto with collision and comprehensive, which the lender likely requires, plus adequate liability. Health insurance adding the baby within the special enrollment period. Term life insurance on both parents to replace income while the child is dependent. Disability insurance, since the self-employed parent has no employer coverage. Professional liability for design errors, and possibly a personal umbrella.

terms.definition: Separate auto liability limits per person, per accident, and for property damage.
The share of covered costs the insured pays after the deductible.
Life insurance for a set period with no cash value.
The waiting time before disability benefits begin.
State-required, no-fault coverage for employees' work-related injuries.

questions.prompt: Which homeowners form is designed for renters?
questions.explanation: HO-4 covers a tenant's belongings and liability.

questions.prompt: Which auto coverage pays for hail damage to the insured's car?
questions.explanation: Comprehensive covers non-collision causes such as weather and theft.

questions.prompt: Medicare Part D covers:
questions.explanation: Part D is the prescription drug benefit.

questions.prompt: A $2,000 bill, a $500 deductible, and 30% coinsurance mean the insured pays:
Title insurance protects against:
questions.explanation: It covers problems in the chain of title that existed before purchase.

modules.title: Insurance principles, underwriting, rates, and claims
modules.summary: The risk management process, legal principles of insurance contracts, regulation, underwriting and rate-making, and a complete claims workflow.

sections.heading: Manage risk before insuring it
paragraphs: Pure risk can only cause a loss, such as a fire. Speculative risk can cause a gain or a loss, such as starting a business. Insurance covers pure risk. A peril is a cause of loss, such as wind. A hazard increases the chance or size of a loss. A physical hazard is a condition such as icy steps. A moral hazard is dishonesty, such as faking a claim. A morale hazard is carelessness because one is insured.

The risk management process identifies risks, measures their frequency and severity, chooses a treatment, and monitors results. Enterprise risk management applies this process across all of an organization's risks, including strategic, financial, operational, and reputational risks.
bullets: Self-insurance is planned retention, often with a fund set aside for expected losses.
A captive insurer is an insurance company owned by the businesses it insures.
Reinsurance is insurance for insurers. Treaty reinsurance covers a whole class of policies automatically; facultative reinsurance covers one risk at a time.

sections.heading: Legal principles and regulation

rows: The insured must suffer a financial loss if the event happens
Insurance restores the insured to the prior financial position, without profit
Both parties must disclose material facts honestly
After paying a claim, the insurer can recover from the party who caused the loss
The covered peril must be the direct cause of the loss
The amounts exchanged are unequal and depend on chance
The insurer writes the policy, so unclear wording is read in favor of the insured
Only the insurer makes a legally enforceable promise

paragraphs: Insurance in the United States is regulated mainly by the states, an arrangement confirmed by the McCarran-Ferguson Act of 1945. Each state has an insurance department; Maryland's is the Maryland Insurance Administration. State regulators license insurers, agents, and adjusters, approve rates and policy forms, and monitor insurer solvency. The National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC) writes model laws that states may adopt. Federal law affects areas such as health insurance and flood insurance.

sections.heading: Underwriting and rate-making
paragraphs: Underwriters decide whether to accept a risk and at what price. They classify applicants into groups with similar expected losses. Adverse selection occurs when people with higher risk are more likely to buy coverage, which underwriting tries to control. Many states allow insurers to use credit-based insurance scores, built from credit report data, for auto and home pricing, while some states restrict them.

Actuaries use statistics to predict losses and set rates. The pure premium is expected losses divided by the number of exposure units. The loss ratio is losses divided by earned premiums. The expense ratio is underwriting expenses divided by written premiums. Their sum is the combined ratio. Below 100% means an underwriting profit; above 100% means the insurer depends on investment income.

Insurance technology now includes telematics devices that measure driving, aerial images for property inspections, and automated claims processing. Each tool raises privacy and fairness questions that regulators review.

example.scenario: An insurer earns $10 million in premiums, pays $6.5 million in losses, and spends $3 million on underwriting expenses.
example.solution: Loss ratio: 6.5 / 10 = 65%. Expense ratio: 3 / 10 = 30%. Combined ratio: 95%, so the insurer made an underwriting profit of 5% before investment income.

sections.heading: Work a claim from notice to settlement
steps: Notice of loss: the insured reports the loss promptly and takes reasonable steps to prevent further damage.
Coverage verification: the adjuster confirms the policy was active and the peril and property are covered, and checks exclusions.
Investigation: photos, reports, receipts, statements, and repair estimates document the loss.
Valuation: the adjuster applies the policy's valuation method, deductible, and limits.
Settlement: the insurer pays, repairs, or denies in writing with reasons.
Subrogation: if another party caused the loss, the insurer seeks recovery.
paragraphs: Actual cash value (ACV) equals replacement cost minus depreciation. A 10-year-old roof with a 20-year life that would cost $12,000 to replace has an ACV of $6,000. A replacement cost policy pays the $12,000 minus the deductible. Injury claims include special damages, which are measurable costs like medical bills and lost wages, and general damages, such as pain and suffering. Most states use comparative negligence, which reduces recovery by the injured person's share of fault. Maryland is one of the few states that still uses contributory negligence, which can bar recovery if the injured person was even partly at fault.

Property policies often contain a coinsurance clause requiring the insured to carry coverage equal to a percent of the property's value. If coverage is too low, the payment is reduced in proportion. Hard fraud is deliberately staging a loss; soft fraud is exaggerating a real claim. Insurers use special investigation units and data analytics to flag patterns.

practice.task: A building is worth $500,000. The policy has an 80% coinsurance clause, a $300,000 limit, and a $1,000 deductible. A fire causes $100,000 of damage. How much does the insurer pay?
practice.answer: Required coverage: 80% x 500,000 = $400,000. The insured carried $300,000, which is 300 / 400 = 75% of the requirement. Payment: 0.75 x 100,000 - 1,000 = $74,000.

sections.heading: Careers and organizations
paragraphs: Producers sell insurance. An agent represents the insurer; a broker represents the buyer. Both need a state license for each line they sell. Other careers include underwriter, claims adjuster, actuary, loss control specialist, and risk manager. Common designations are the CPCU (Chartered Property Casualty Underwriter) and ARM (Associate in Risk Management) from The Institutes, the CLU (Chartered Life Underwriter) and ChFC from The American College, and actuarial credentials from the Casualty Actuarial Society and the Society of Actuaries. Industry groups include the NAIC, the Insurance Information Institute, and RIMS for risk managers.

terms.definition: The insurer's right to recover a paid claim from the party who caused the loss.
The tendency of higher-risk people to seek more insurance.
Loss ratio plus expense ratio; below 100% shows an underwriting profit.
Replacement cost minus depreciation.
An insurance company owned by the organizations it insures.

questions.prompt: A risk with low frequency and high severity is usually best:
questions.explanation: Rare but costly losses are the classic use of insurance.

questions.prompt: Which principle prevents an insured from profiting from a loss?
questions.explanation: Indemnity restores the prior position without gain.

questions.prompt: Insurance in the United States is regulated mainly by:
questions.explanation: The NAIC writes model laws, but states hold regulatory authority.

questions.prompt: Losses are $7 million, earned premiums $10 million, and the expense ratio 28%. The combined ratio is:
questions.explanation: 70% loss ratio + 28% expense ratio = 98%.

questions.prompt: Exaggerating the value of items stolen in a real burglary is:
questions.explanation: Soft fraud inflates a legitimate claim.

modules.title: Everyday money tasks: pay, taxes, banking, credit, and protection
modules.summary: Read a pay stub, work a simplified tax return, reconcile a bank account, manage credit and identity theft, and plan saving and protection.

sections.heading: Read a pay stub
paragraphs: A pay stub shows gross pay, then pre-tax deductions such as retirement contributions and health premiums, then taxes withheld, then after-tax deductions, and finally net pay. Each line usually shows the current period and the year-to-date (YTD) total. Check the hours, rate, and YTD totals every pay period. Errors are easier to fix right away.

Income comes from wages and salary, tips, self-employment, interest, dividends, capital gains, rent, and government benefits. Earned income comes from work. Unearned income comes from investments and other sources, and some is taxed differently.

sections.heading: Work a simplified tax return
paragraphs: The real Form 1040 changes every year. This example uses practice numbers chosen for easy math, not the official 2026 brackets or deduction. On a test, use the figures given.

The return follows a fixed order. Total income minus adjustments, such as deductible IRA contributions, gives adjusted gross income (AGI). AGI minus the standard deduction or itemized deductions gives taxable income. The tax comes from the brackets. Credits reduce the tax dollar for dollar. Finally, compare the tax with what was withheld or paid. The difference is a refund or an amount owed.

example.scenario: A single filer earns $30,000 in wages, has no adjustments, takes a practice standard deduction of $16,000, and had $1,700 withheld. Practice brackets: 10% on the first $12,000 of taxable income and 12% above that.
example.solution: The refund is $260. The marginal rate, which applies to the last dollar, is 12%. The effective rate is 1,440 / 30,000 = 4.8% of total income. Moving into a higher bracket raises the tax only on the income above the bracket line.

sections.heading: Reconcile a bank account
paragraphs: A bank reconciliation explains why the bank statement and the account register show different balances. Adjust the bank balance for items the bank has not seen yet: add deposits in transit and subtract outstanding checks. Adjust the register for items only the bank knew about: subtract service fees and returned checks, and add interest earned. Both adjusted balances must match.

example.scenario: The statement shows $1,240. A $300 deposit made on the last day is not on it. Checks for $85 and $140 have not cleared. The register shows $1,300. The statement shows a $10 fee and $25 of interest that are not in the register.
steps: Adjusted bank balance: 1,240 + 300 - 85 - 140 = 1,315.
Adjusted register balance: 1,300 - 10 + 25 = 1,315.
example.solution: Both equal $1,315, so the account is reconciled. Record the fee and the interest in the register.

sections.heading: Credit, borrowing, and identity theft
paragraphs: Credit reports come from three national bureaus: Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion. Everyone can get free reports weekly at AnnualCreditReport.com. A FICO score weighs payment history (35%), amounts owed (30%), length of credit history (15%), new credit (10%), and credit mix (10%). Paying on time and keeping card balances low relative to limits matter most.

Revolving credit, such as a credit card, can be reused up to a limit. Installment credit, such as an auto loan, is repaid in fixed payments. Compare loans by APR and total cost. A $2,000 card balance at 24% APR accrues about $40 of interest in one month (2,000 x 0.24 / 12). Paying only the minimum can stretch repayment over years.

If identity theft is suspected, report it at IdentityTheft.gov, place a fraud alert or a free credit freeze with each bureau, change passwords, and review statements and reports. A freeze stops new accounts from being opened in your name until you lift it.

sections.heading: Net worth, saving, and protection
paragraphs: Net worth equals assets minus liabilities. Track it once or twice a year. Compound growth rewards starting early: at 7%, money doubles about every 10 years by the rule of 72. An emergency fund of three to six months of essential expenses comes before most investing.

Protection includes insurance (health, auto, renters or home, disability, and life if others depend on your income) and basic estate documents. A will names who receives property and who cares for minor children. Beneficiary designations on retirement accounts and life insurance override a will for those accounts, so keep them current. A durable power of attorney and a health care directive name people to act if you cannot. Charitable giving can follow a budget line, and tax rules for deducting gifts change, so check the current year's rules.

practice.task: Jordan, 24, earns $3,200 a month after taxes. Expenses are rent $1,100, car payment $350, other essentials $900, and $400 of discretionary spending. Jordan has $1,500 in savings, a $4,000 card balance at 22% APR, a $9,000 car loan at 6%, and a car worth $11,000. (a) What is Jordan's net worth? (b) How much is left each month? (c) Recommend an order for using it.
practice.answer: (a) Assets 1,500 + 11,000 = 12,500; liabilities 4,000 + 9,000 = 13,000; net worth -$500. (b) 3,200 - 1,100 - 350 - 900 - 400 = $450 a month. (c) Build a small starter emergency fund, then put most of the $450 on the 22% card while paying all minimums. Once the card is paid, grow the emergency fund toward three months of essentials (about $7,050 for rent, car, and essentials), then increase retirement saving.

terms.definition: Total income minus certain adjustments; the starting point for deductions.
The rate applied to the next dollar of taxable income.
A deposit recorded by the account holder that has not yet appeared on the bank statement.
A free block on new credit accounts being opened using your credit report.
Total assets minus total liabilities.

questions.prompt: A tax credit of $500 reduces a $2,000 tax bill to:
questions.explanation: Credits reduce tax dollar for dollar.

questions.prompt: In a bank reconciliation, an outstanding check is:
questions.explanation: The bank has not paid it yet, so the statement balance is too high.

questions.prompt: Which factor carries the most weight in a FICO score?
questions.explanation: Payment history is about 35% of the score.

questions.prompt: A retirement account's beneficiary designation and a will name different people. Who receives the account?
choices: The person named in the will
questions.explanation: Beneficiary designations generally control those accounts.

questions.prompt: Using the rule of 72, money earning 9% doubles in about:
questions.explanation: Divide 72 by the rate: 72 / 9 = 8 years.

modules.title: Financial planning case method: from fact-finding to recommendations
modules.summary: Organize a household's facts, measure its position, compare alternatives for each goal, and present dated, supported recommendations.

sections.heading: Gather and organize the facts
paragraphs: This lesson uses the fictional Rivera household to show the method. It is not the competition case. Start by sorting every fact into a table before making any recommendation. Mark facts that are missing and state the assumption you will use instead.

The Riveras are a married couple, ages 38 and 36, with two children ages 6 and 10. They take home $7,400 a month. They have $4,000 in checking and savings, $52,000 in workplace retirement accounts, a home worth $340,000 with a $255,000 mortgage, a car worth $14,000 with a $9,000 loan, and $11,000 of credit card debt across two cards. One spouse has employer life insurance equal to one year of salary; the other has none. They want to rebuild savings after a job loss, pay off the cards, and start saving for college.

rows: Gross pay and tax withholding not given
Mortgage $1,850; car $300; minimums $330; other essentials $3,400; discretionary $900
Assume spending is accurate; ask for 3 months of statements
Mortgage $255,000 at 6%; car $9,000 at 7%; Card A $8,000 at 24%; Card B $3,000 at 18%
Employer life on one spouse only; no disability coverage listed
Emergency fund, eliminate card debt, college saving
Ask for target dates and amounts

sections.heading: Measure the starting position
paragraphs: Build a personal balance sheet and a monthly cash flow statement, then compute a few standard measures. Use them to set priorities, not to judge the family.
steps: Essential monthly expenses: 1,850 + 300 + 330 + 3,400 = $5,880.
Emergency fund coverage: 4,000 / 5,880 = 0.7 months, below the common 3 to 6 month guideline.
Credit card interest: 8,000 x 24% / 12 + 3,000 x 18% / 12 = 160 + 45 = about $205 a month.

sections.heading: Compare alternatives for each goal
paragraphs: For each goal, list at least two options with their costs, risks, and tradeoffs. The debt avalanche pays extra on the highest-rate debt first and costs the least interest. The debt snowball pays the smallest balance first and gives a quicker win, which helps some families stay motivated. Here the avalanche targets Card A (24%) and the snowball targets Card B ($3,000).

rows: Keep $1,000 starter fund, then build after cards
Could save most interest for a set period
Transfer fee, often 3% to 5%; rate jumps afterward; requires good credit
Tax-free growth for qualified education costs
Penalty and tax on earnings for nonqualified withdrawals
Low cost while children are dependent

bullets: Retirement: do not reduce contributions below the level that earns the full employer match, because the match is an immediate return.
State assumptions with dates, for example: rates as of November 2026, a 6% assumed long-term return, and 3% inflation.

sections.heading: Write and present the recommendations
paragraphs: Write each recommendation as: the goal, the action, the numbers, the reason, and when to review it. Then show how the recommendations fit together in one monthly budget so they do not spend the same $620 twice.

Say when a qualified professional is needed. An attorney drafts wills and guardianship documents, a tax professional handles complex returns, and a licensed insurance agent or fee-only planner can price specific policies. Name review triggers such as a job change, a new child, a large raise, a move, or a major market drop.

example.scenario: Show one complete recommendation for the Riveras' card debt.
example.solution: Goal: eliminate $11,000 of card debt. Action: keep paying all minimums, cut discretionary spending by $200, and send the $620 surplus plus $200 to Card A until it is paid, then roll that amount to Card B. Numbers: about $1,150 a month goes to the cards (the $330 of minimums plus $820 extra), which clears both cards in about 11 months if no new charges are made. Reason: Card A's 24% rate is the costliest debt. Review: monthly, and stop new card charges. If credit allows, compare a balance transfer including its fee.

practice.task: Using the Rivera facts, write one recommendation for life insurance. Include the action, a reasoned coverage estimate, the reason, and a review trigger.
practice.answer: A strong answer recommends level term life insurance on both spouses, since the children are 6 and 10. A simple estimate covers debts (about $275,000), several years of income replacement, and college goals, then subtracts existing coverage. The term should last until the youngest child is independent, about 15 to 20 years. The reason is that term life is the lowest-cost way to protect dependents' income. Review after a raise, a new child, or the mortgage payoff. The answer should say that exact quotes come from a licensed agent.

terms.definition: A summary of a household's income and spending over a period.
Paying extra toward the highest-interest debt first.
Paying extra toward the smallest balance first.
A life or market event that should prompt a plan update.
A state-sponsored education savings account with tax-free growth for qualified costs.

questions.prompt: Essential expenses are $4,000 a month and savings are $6,000. Emergency fund coverage is:
Which method minimizes total interest paid on multiple debts?
questions.explanation: Targeting the highest rate first saves the most interest.

questions.prompt: Why should a planner state assumptions with a date?
choices: Rates and rules change, so readers know when figures were current
It is required by FBLA bylaws
questions.explanation: Dated assumptions show what the recommendation depended on.

questions.prompt: Which professional should draft a guardianship designation for minor children?
questions.explanation: Wills and guardianship documents are legal documents.

questions.prompt: Before cutting retirement contributions to pay debt, a planner first checks:
choices: Whether contributions earn an employer match
questions.explanation: Giving up a match gives up an immediate return.

modules.title: Researching a public company from its filings
modules.summary: Find and read a 10-K, use the notes and MD&A, analyze all four statements across years, and support strategic recommendations with evidence.

sections.heading: Find the right documents
paragraphs: Public companies file reports on the SEC's EDGAR system. Search by company name or ticker, then filter by form type. Confirm the company's fiscal year end on the cover page, since many retailers end their year in a month other than December. Use the filing for the fiscal year the event names, and record the filing date and URL for every number you use.
This lesson uses a fictional retailer, Harbor Wholesale, to teach the method. Students research the assigned company on their own.

sections.heading: Read the 10-K in a useful order
steps: Item 1, Business: what the company sells, how it earns money, its segments, and its competition.
Item 1A, Risk Factors: management's own list of what could harm results.
Item 7, MD&A: management's explanation of why results changed, often with comparable sales and other operating measures.
Item 8, Financial Statements and notes: the income statement, balance sheet, cash flow statement, and statement of shareholders' equity, plus the auditor's report.
The notes: accounting policies for revenue, inventory, leases, and segments. These explain how the numbers were measured.
paragraphs: The statement of shareholders' equity shows why equity changed: net income added, dividends subtracted, share repurchases subtracted, stock-based compensation added, and other comprehensive income. A company can grow net income while equity falls if it returns large amounts to shareholders.

sections.heading: Analyze across periods and against peers
paragraphs: Calculate each ratio for at least three years so you see a trend. Put the calculations in a spreadsheet with a cell reference to each source number. Retailers are usually judged on gross margin, operating expenses as a percent of sales, inventory turnover, comparable sales growth, and return on invested capital. Compare the company with two or three competitors that sell similar goods to similar customers.

example.scenario: Harbor Wholesale reports (in millions): Year 1 revenue 40,000, gross profit 5,200, SG&A 3,800, net income 1,000. Year 2 revenue 44,000, gross profit 5,500, SG&A 4,000, net income 1,150. Cost of sales in Year 2 is 38,500, and average inventory is 3,850.
steps: SG&A as percent of revenue: Year 1 9.5%; Year 2 9.1%.
Net margin: Year 1 2.5%; Year 2 2.6%.
Inventory turnover, Year 2: 38,500 / 3,850 = 10 times, or about 36.5 days.
example.solution: Harbor grew sales 10% while gross margin slipped half a point, likely from lower prices or higher product costs. It offset that by spreading operating costs over more sales, so net margin rose slightly. Next, check MD&A for the stated cause and compare peers' margins before drawing a conclusion.

sections.heading: Recommend strategic actions
paragraphs: A strong recommendation connects one finding to one action and states the expected effect, the risk, and how it would be measured. Limit the analysis to two or three actions that the evidence supports. State limitations, such as the use of one fiscal year, differences in competitors' fiscal calendars, or figures that management chooses to report without audit.

practice.task: Using the Harbor figures, write one strategic recommendation in four parts: finding, action, expected effect, and risk.
practice.answer: Sample: Finding: gross margin fell from 13.0% to 12.5% as revenue grew 10%. Action: review pricing and supplier costs in the categories with the largest margin decline, and expand higher-margin private-label products. Expected effect: recover part of the margin while keeping prices competitive, measured by category gross margin over the next four quarters. Risk: raising prices or narrowing selection could slow sales growth, so test changes in a few categories first.

terms.definition: The SEC's public database of company filings.
Management's discussion and analysis: management's explanation of results in the 10-K.
A company's 12-month accounting year, which may not match the calendar year.
Sales growth from stores open long enough to compare with the prior period.
A statement explaining the changes in each equity account during the period.

questions.prompt: Which filing contains a company's audited annual financial statements?
questions.explanation: The 10-K is the annual report with audited statements.

questions.prompt: Where does management explain why results changed?
questions.explanation: MD&A discusses results, trends, and causes.

questions.prompt: Revenue rose from $50 billion to $54 billion. Growth was:
questions.explanation: Change divided by the starting value: (54 - 50) / 50 = 8%.

questions.prompt: Large share repurchases affect shareholders' equity by:
questions.explanation: Buybacks return cash to owners and reduce equity.

questions.prompt: Which note would explain the inventory costing method?
questions.explanation: The accounting policies note describes how inventory and other items are measured.

modules.title: Applied economics: utility, production, costs, and indicators
modules.summary: Classify economic resources and utility, calculate productivity, diminishing returns, cost and profit, elasticity, and inflation, and read the business cycle.

sections.heading: Resources, goods, and utility
paragraphs: The four factors of production are land (natural resources), labor (human effort), capital (tools, machines, and buildings used to make other goods), and entrepreneurship (organizing the other three and taking risk). Money is not capital in this sense; it buys capital. Goods are tangible. Services are intangible, are produced and consumed at the same time, and cannot be stored.
Utility is the usefulness that makes people willing to pay. Businesses add value by creating each type.

rows: Changing raw materials into a product
A bakery turns flour into bread
Making a product available where customers are
A vending machine in a gym
Making a product available when customers want it
Making it easier to own or use the product

bullets: Business activities are often grouped as extractive (farming, mining), production or manufacturing, marketing and merchandising (wholesale and retail), and services.
Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up. It applies to every choice, including a business's use of time.

sections.heading: Productivity, specialization, and diminishing returns
paragraphs: Productivity is output divided by input. If 12 workers produce 960 units in an 8-hour shift, labor productivity is 960 / (12 x 8) = 10 units per labor hour. If new equipment raises output to 1,152 units with the same workers, productivity rises to 12 units per hour, a 20% increase. Higher productivity lets a business pay more or charge less without losing profit.

Specialization means each worker or business concentrates on a narrow task. Division of labor splits production into steps. Adam Smith's pin factory example showed that workers each doing one step produce far more than workers each making whole pins. Specialization raises skill and speed but can make work repetitive and create dependence on others.

The law of diminishing returns says that adding more of one input while others stay fixed eventually adds less and less output. It applies in the short run, when something such as factory space cannot change.
bullets: Marginal output rises with the second worker because two workers can share tasks. It falls after that because the fixed space and equipment become crowded.

Organized labor is workers acting together through unions. Unions negotiate wages, benefits, and conditions through collective bargaining. The National Labor Relations Act of 1935 protects the right to organize. The Taft-Hartley Act of 1947 allowed states to pass right-to-work laws.

sections.heading: Cost and profit
paragraphs: Fixed costs stay the same at any output level in the short run. Variable costs change with output. Total cost is fixed plus variable. Marginal cost is the added cost of producing one more unit. A business earns the most profit by producing until marginal revenue equals marginal cost. Under perfect competition, marginal revenue equals the price.

example.scenario: A shop sells candles for $18 each. Fixed cost is $200. Total cost is $320 at 10 candles, $420 at 20, $540 at 30, $700 at 40, and $900 at 50. Which output earns the most profit?
steps: Marginal cost per candle for each block of 10: (320 - 200) / 10 = 12; then 10; then 12; then 16; then 20.
Profit at each level: 10 candles 180 - 320 = -140; 20 candles 360 - 420 = -60; 30 candles 540 - 540 = 0; 40 candles 720 - 700 = 20; 50 candles 900 - 900 = 0.
From 40 to 50 candles, marginal cost ($20) is greater than the $18 price, so those candles lose money.
example.solution: Profit is highest at 40 candles. The last block made has a marginal cost of $16, below the price, and the next block would cost more than it brings in.

sections.heading: Elasticity and economic indicators
paragraphs: Price elasticity of demand equals the percent change in quantity demanded divided by the percent change in price. If price rises from $10 to $11 (10%) and quantity falls from 1,000 to 850 (15%), elasticity is 1.5, so demand is elastic. Revenue falls from $10,000 to $9,350. When demand is inelastic, below 1, a price increase raises revenue. Necessities with few substitutes, such as insulin, tend to be inelastic.

Gross domestic product (GDP) is the market value of final goods and services produced in a country in a year: consumption + investment + government spending + net exports. Real GDP removes inflation; nominal GDP does not. The inflation rate is the percent change in the Consumer Price Index: a CPI rising from 300 to 309 means 3% inflation. The unemployment rate is the number of unemployed people looking for work divided by the labor force.

The business cycle moves through expansion, peak, contraction, and trough. A recession is a significant, widespread decline in activity. Leading indicators, such as building permits, stock prices, and new jobless claims, tend to change before the economy does. Coincident indicators, such as employment and industrial production, move with it. Lagging indicators, such as the length of unemployment, change afterward.
bullets: Fiscal policy is government taxing and spending, set by Congress and the President. Monetary policy is the Federal Reserve's control of interest rates and the money supply.
Higher interest rates raise borrowing costs, slow consumer spending on cars and homes, and reduce business investment.
Government affects business through regulation, taxes, spending, and antitrust laws: the Sherman Act (1890), the Clayton Act (1914), and the Federal Trade Commission Act (1914).

practice.task: A coffee shop raises its latte price from $5.00 to $5.50, and daily sales fall from 400 to 380. (a) Calculate the price elasticity. (b) Is demand elastic or inelastic? (c) What happened to daily revenue?
practice.answer: (a) Price change: 0.50 / 5.00 = 10%. Quantity change: 20 / 400 = 5%. Elasticity: 5 / 10 = 0.5. (b) Inelastic, because it is below 1. (c) Revenue rose from 400 x 5.00 = $2,000 to 380 x 5.50 = $2,090.

modules.title: Economic systems, ownership, and business models
modules.summary: Compare economic systems and market structures, choose a form of ownership, connect business functions, and describe how a business earns money.

sections.heading: Economic systems and private enterprise
paragraphs: Every economy answers what to produce, how to produce it, and for whom. A traditional economy relies on custom. A command economy relies on government planning. A market economy relies on individual choices and prices. Most countries, including the United States, have mixed economies that combine markets with some government role.

The U.S. private enterprise system rests on private property, the profit motive, competition, and freedom of choice. Profit rewards businesses for taking risk and meeting needs. Competition pushes businesses to improve quality and lower prices. Risk is the possibility of loss. Economic risks come from changes in the economy or competition, natural risks from weather and disasters, and human risks from theft, errors, or poor decisions.

sections.heading: Forms of ownership

paragraphs: A franchise is a licensing arrangement, not a separate legal form. The franchisee buys the right to use the franchisor's name, products, and system, pays an initial fee and ongoing royalties, and follows the franchisor's rules. The franchisee gets a proven model and loses some independence.

sections.heading: How the business functions connect
paragraphs: Each business function depends on the others. A decision in one creates work in the rest. Tests often describe a task and ask which function performs it.

example.scenario: A small bicycle shop decides to add electric bikes. Trace the effects across functions.
example.solution: Marketing researches demand and sets prices. Finance arranges money for inventory and checks the cash flow effect. Operations finds suppliers and adds a charging and repair area. HR trains mechanics on batteries and safety. Accounting tracks the new product line's margin. Information management adds the bikes to the point-of-sale and inventory system. Management sets the goal and reviews results.

sections.heading: Business models and organizational design
paragraphs: A business model explains how a company creates value for customers and earns money. A subscription model charges a recurring fee, such as a meal kit service. A freemium model gives basic features free and charges for upgrades. A marketplace or platform connects buyers and sellers and takes a fee. An advertising model offers free content and sells audience attention. A licensing model charges others to use intellectual property.

Organizational design is the structure of jobs and reporting lines. A functional structure groups people by specialty, such as marketing or finance. A divisional structure groups by product, customer, or region. A matrix structure gives employees two bosses, a functional manager and a project manager. A flat structure has few management levels and wide spans of control, which speeds decisions but stretches managers.

Businesses must adapt when markets change. Signs that change is needed include falling sales, new competitors, new technology, and shifting customer habits. Adaptation can mean new products, new channels, or a new model, such as a video rental chain moving to streaming.

practice.task: Two friends will open a food truck. One will run it; the other will invest $20,000 but not work there. They want to protect their personal savings from lawsuits. Recommend a form of ownership and explain why two alternatives fit less well.
practice.answer: An LLC fits: both owners get limited liability, profits usually pass through to their personal returns, and the operating agreement can give the managing owner control while the investor's role stays limited. A general partnership would expose both to unlimited liability. A C corporation offers protection but adds double taxation and more formalities than a single food truck needs.

A market with a few large sellers who watch and react to each other.

modules.title: International trade: law, documents, alliances, and culture
modules.summary: Import and export procedures and records, export controls, trade agreements, exchange rates, anti-bribery law, culture, and business travel.

sections.heading: Why countries trade
paragraphs: A country has an absolute advantage when it can produce more of a good with the same resources. It has a comparative advantage when its opportunity cost of producing a good is lower. Trade benefits both sides when each specializes in its comparative advantage, even if one country is better at producing everything.

Trade barriers include tariffs (taxes on imports), quotas (limits on quantity), embargoes (bans on trade with a country), subsidies to domestic producers, and nontariff barriers such as product standards and licensing rules. The balance of trade is exports minus imports. A trade deficit means a country imports more than it exports.

example.scenario: Country A can make 10 laptops or 20 shirts per worker-day. Country B can make 2 laptops or 10 shirts.
example.solution: Country A has an absolute advantage in both. Its opportunity cost of one laptop is 2 shirts, while B's is 5 shirts. B's opportunity cost of one shirt is 0.2 laptops versus A's 0.5. A should specialize in laptops and B in shirts, then trade.

sections.heading: Exchange rates in practice
paragraphs: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in another. If 1 euro equals 1.10 dollars, then 1 dollar equals 1 / 1.10 = 0.909 euro. A 500-euro item costs an American buyer 500 x 1.10 = $550. When the dollar strengthens to 1 euro = 1.00 dollar, the same item costs $500. A strong dollar makes imports cheaper for Americans and makes American exports more expensive abroad.

Exchange rates change with interest rates, inflation, trade flows, and political stability. A business that will pay or receive foreign currency later faces exchange-rate risk and may use a forward contract to lock in a rate.

practice.task: A U.S. company sells machine parts for 2,000,000 yen. When the order is signed, $1 = 150 yen. When payment arrives, $1 = 160 yen. How many dollars did the company expect, and how many did it receive?
practice.answer: Expected: 2,000,000 / 150 = $13,333. Received: 2,000,000 / 160 = $12,500. The yen weakened, so the company received $833 less. A forward contract could have locked in the original rate.

sections.heading: Import and export procedures
paragraphs: Importers classify goods using the Harmonized Tariff Schedule (HTS), which sets the duty rate. Most duties are ad valorem, a percent of value: a $20,000 shipment with a 4% duty owes $800. U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) processes entries, collects duties, and enforces trade laws. Many importers hire a licensed customs broker.

Exporters must check whether a license is required. The Export Administration Regulations (EAR), run by the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, cover commercial and dual-use items. The International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR), run by the State Department, cover defense items. The Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) enforces sanctions on countries and persons. Most exports need Electronic Export Information filed in the Automated Export System when a shipment's value is over $2,500 per commodity classification or a license is required.

CIF (Cost, Insurance, and Freight): seller pays freight and insurance to the destination port. DDP (Delivered Duty Paid): seller handles everything, including import duties.

paragraphs: A free trade area removes tariffs among members. A customs union also sets a common tariff toward outsiders. A common market adds free movement of labor and capital. Geography, history, and development level shape trade: landlocked countries face higher shipping costs, former colonial ties often shape language and trade partners, and developing economies may compete on labor costs while building infrastructure.

sections.heading: Bribery, labor, and culture
paragraphs: The Foreign Corrupt Practices Act of 1977 makes it illegal for U.S. companies and people to bribe foreign officials to win or keep business. It also requires public companies to keep accurate books and internal controls. It contains a narrow exception for small facilitating payments to speed routine government actions, such as processing paperwork. The United Kingdom's Bribery Act has no such exception. Many companies ban facilitating payments entirely.

Global labor issues include child labor, forced labor, unsafe conditions, and low wages in supply chains. The International Labour Organization sets core standards. U.S. law blocks imports made with forced labor, so importers audit suppliers.

Culture affects negotiation, management, and marketing. In low-context cultures such as the United States and Germany, people state meaning directly in words. In high-context cultures such as Japan and much of the Middle East, meaning depends on relationships, setting, and nonverbal cues. Hofstede's dimensions compare countries on power distance, individualism, uncertainty avoidance, achievement orientation, long-term orientation, and indulgence. Use them as starting points, since individuals vary.
bullets: Business travel requires a valid passport, the right visa for business activity, and attention to State Department travel advisories.

modules.title: Sources of law, courts, procedure, and torts
modules.summary: Classify sources of law, follow a case through the courts, compare alternative dispute resolution, explain administrative law, and analyze torts and remedies.

sections.heading: Sources and types of law
paragraphs: The U.S. Constitution is the highest law; a statute or rule that conflicts with it is invalid. Statutes are laws passed by Congress or state legislatures. Administrative regulations are rules issued by agencies under authority given by statutes. Case law, or common law, comes from court decisions. Courts follow precedent under the doctrine of stare decisis, so similar cases are decided in similar ways. Treaties and executive orders are also sources.

Criminal law deals with wrongs against society, prosecuted by the government, with punishment such as fines or prison. Civil law deals with disputes between private parties, usually seeking money damages. The same act can lead to both: an assault can bring a criminal charge and a civil suit. The burden of proof differs. Criminal cases require proof beyond a reasonable doubt; most civil cases require a preponderance of the evidence, meaning more likely than not.
Substantive law defines rights and duties, such as what makes a contract valid. Procedural law sets the steps for enforcing them, such as how to file a lawsuit.

sections.heading: The court system
paragraphs: Federal courts hear cases involving federal law or the Constitution (federal question jurisdiction) and cases between citizens of different states when more than $75,000 is at stake (diversity jurisdiction). Federal district courts are trial courts. The 13 federal circuit courts of appeals review district court decisions. The U.S. Supreme Court hears a small number of appeals it chooses to accept.

State courts hear most cases, including contract, property, family, and most criminal cases. Maryland's trial courts are the District Court and the Circuit Courts. Appeals go to the Appellate Court of Maryland and then to the Supreme Court of Maryland. Those two courts were renamed in 2022; older materials call them the Court of Special Appeals and the Court of Appeals.
Trial courts decide facts and apply law, often with juries. Appellate courts review the record for legal errors and do not hear new witnesses.
steps: The plaintiff files a complaint, and the defendant is served with a summons.
The defendant files an answer, which may include a counterclaim, or a motion to dismiss.
Discovery: the parties exchange evidence through depositions (sworn oral questioning), interrogatories (written questions), and requests for documents.
Pretrial motions and conferences may narrow the issues or lead to settlement. Most civil cases settle.
Trial: jury selection, opening statements, presentation of evidence, closing arguments, jury instructions, and verdict.
Judgment and possible appeal.

paragraphs: Administrative agencies such as the EPA, OSHA, and the FTC are created by enabling statutes. They make rules, enforce them, and decide disputes. Under the Administrative Procedure Act, most federal rules follow notice-and-comment rulemaking: the agency publishes a proposed rule in the Federal Register, accepts public comments, and then publishes the final rule. Administrative law judges hear agency enforcement cases, and their decisions can be appealed to courts.

sections.heading: Torts and remedies
paragraphs: A tort is a civil wrong, other than a breach of contract, that causes harm. Intentional torts include battery (harmful contact), assault (threat of immediate harm), false imprisonment, defamation (false statements harming reputation; libel is written and slander is spoken), invasion of privacy, trespass, conversion (taking someone's personal property), and fraud. Business torts include interfering with another's contract and unfair competition.

Negligence is failing to use reasonable care. The plaintiff must prove four elements: a duty of care, a breach of that duty, causation (the breach actually and foreseeably caused the harm), and damages. Defenses include assumption of risk and the plaintiff's own negligence. Most states use comparative negligence, which reduces damages by the plaintiff's share of fault. Maryland uses contributory negligence, which can bar recovery entirely. Strict liability applies without proof of fault to abnormally dangerous activities and to defective products.

Remedies at law are money damages. Compensatory damages repay actual losses. Punitive damages punish especially bad conduct. Nominal damages, such as $1, recognize a wrong without real loss. Equitable remedies include an injunction (a court order to do or stop doing something), specific performance (ordering a party to perform a contract, usually for unique items like land), and rescission (undoing a contract).

example.scenario: A grocery employee mops a floor and leaves no warning sign. A customer slips and breaks a wrist, missing two weeks of work.
example.solution: This is a negligence claim. The store owes customers a duty of reasonable care, leaving a wet floor unmarked is a breach, the fall was caused by the wet floor, and the customer has damages (medical bills and lost wages). The store would raise any carelessness by the customer; in Maryland, contributory negligence could bar recovery if the customer was partly at fault. This is civil law, and the store is liable for its employee's act within the scope of employment.

practice.task: Classify each case by type of law and court. (a) A Maryland bakery sues a Maryland supplier for $40,000 over spoiled flour. (b) A Virginia company sues a Maryland company for $200,000 over a contract. (c) A business is charged with violating a federal environmental statute. (d) Two partners agree to have a neutral expert hear their dispute and issue a final decision.
practice.answer: (a) Civil contract case in Maryland state court, since both parties are in Maryland and no federal law is involved. (b) Civil; it can be heard in federal district court under diversity jurisdiction because the parties are from different states and more than $75,000 is at stake, or in state court. (c) Criminal or civil enforcement under federal law, heard in federal court. (d) Binding arbitration, a form of alternative dispute resolution.

modules.title: Commercial, employment, consumer, and regulatory law
modules.summary: Agency, secured transactions and bankruptcy, intellectual property, environmental and consumer protection, employment law, and tax and financial law.

sections.heading: Agency
paragraphs: In an agency relationship, an agent acts on behalf of a principal. Agency can be created by express agreement, by implication from conduct, or by ratification when a principal approves an unauthorized act afterward. An agent has actual authority (express or implied) when the principal grants it, and apparent authority when the principal's conduct leads a third party to reasonably believe the agent has authority.

An agent owes the principal duties of loyalty (no secret profits or competing), obedience, reasonable care, accounting for money, and notification of important information. The principal owes the agent compensation, reimbursement of proper expenses, indemnification, and cooperation.

Under respondeat superior, an employer is liable for torts its employees commit within the scope of employment. A business is generally not liable for the torts of independent contractors, so the distinction matters. Signs of employee status include the employer controlling how and when work is done, providing tools, and paying regularly.

sections.heading: Debtors, creditors, and the UCC
paragraphs: The Uniform Commercial Code (UCC), adopted in some form by every state, governs commercial transactions. Article 2 covers the sale of goods, Article 3 covers negotiable instruments such as checks and notes, and Article 9 covers secured transactions.

A secured creditor holds a security interest in specific collateral. The interest attaches when there is a security agreement, the creditor gives value, and the debtor has rights in the collateral. The creditor usually perfects the interest by filing a financing statement with the state, which gives priority over later creditors. An unsecured creditor has only a general claim.

Other creditor remedies include liens (a mechanic's lien for work on real property, an artisan's lien for repairs to personal property, and a judgment lien) and garnishment, a court order directing a third party such as an employer to pay part of the debtor's wages to the creditor. A guarantor pays only if the debtor fails and the creditor first tries to collect from the debtor; a surety is directly liable from the start.

Bankruptcy is federal law. Chapter 7 liquidates nonexempt assets to pay creditors and discharges most remaining debts. Chapter 11 lets a business reorganize and keep operating. Chapter 13 lets individuals with regular income keep property under a three-to-five-year repayment plan. Filing creates an automatic stay that stops most collection actions.

paragraphs: Ideas and facts alone are not copyrightable. A business chooses protection based on the asset. A patent requires public disclosure, so some companies keep processes as trade secrets instead. Infringement remedies include injunctions and damages.

sections.heading: Environmental and consumer protection
paragraphs: The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) enforces most federal environmental laws. The National Environmental Policy Act requires environmental impact statements for major federal actions. The Clean Air Act and Clean Water Act set pollution limits. The Resource Conservation and Recovery Act regulates hazardous waste from creation to disposal. CERCLA, the Superfund law, can make current and past owners of contaminated sites liable for cleanup even if they did not cause the pollution.

The Federal Trade Commission Act bans unfair or deceptive acts and practices. The Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act sets rules for written consumer warranties. The Consumer Product Safety Commission sets safety standards and orders recalls. The Fair Debt Collection Practices Act limits how third-party debt collectors may act, such as banning harassment and calls at unusual hours. The Fair Credit Billing Act lets consumers dispute billing errors on credit cards. The FTC's Cooling-Off Rule gives buyers three days to cancel certain sales made at the buyer's home or at temporary locations. State lemon laws give remedies for new cars with repeated defects.

paragraphs: Most U.S. employment, including in Maryland, is at will: either side may end it at any time for any lawful reason. Exceptions include contracts, discrimination laws, retaliation for protected activity, and firings that violate public policy, such as firing someone for serving on a jury.

Financial law includes securities laws, the Sarbanes-Oxley Act's reporting and audit rules, the Dodd-Frank Act, and consumer credit laws such as the Truth in Lending Act and the Credit CARD Act of 2009. Taxes include income taxes (progressive, rising with income), payroll taxes, sales taxes (regressive, taking a larger share of a low income), excise taxes on specific goods, property taxes, estate taxes, and tariffs. Tax avoidance uses legal methods to lower taxes. Tax evasion, such as hiding income, is a crime.

practice.task: Identify the legal issue and the relevant law. (a) A delivery driver for a florist runs a red light during a delivery and hits a car. (b) A collection agency calls a debtor at 11 p.m. several nights in a row. (c) A company fires a 58-year-old manager and replaces her with a 30-year-old, citing "fresh energy." (d) A rival hires a chef and obtains a restaurant's secret sauce recipe.
practice.answer: (a) Agency and respondeat superior: the florist is likely liable because the driver was an employee acting within the scope of employment. (b) The Fair Debt Collection Practices Act bars calls at unusual or inconvenient times, generally before 8 a.m. or after 9 p.m. (c) Possible age discrimination under the ADEA, which protects workers 40 and older. (d) Trade secret misappropriation, if the restaurant took reasonable steps to keep the recipe secret.

example.scenario: A software startup wants to protect its app name, its source code, and a new data compression method.
example.solution: Register the app name as a trademark. The source code is automatically copyrighted when written; registering it allows a lawsuit and statutory damages. The compression method may be patentable if it is new and non-obvious, or it could be kept as a trade secret if it can stay hidden from users.

paragraphs: Six Sigma aims for no more than 3.4 defects per million opportunities. Lean targets waste such as waiting, excess inventory, unnecessary movement, overproduction, and defects. Both use data, but Lean emphasizes speed and flow while Six Sigma emphasizes reducing variation.

sections.heading: Map a process and find the bottleneck
paragraphs: A workflow diagram shows each step, who does it, and how work moves. A process can go no faster than its slowest step, the bottleneck. Improving any other step does not raise output.

example.scenario: A print shop's order process has four steps with these hourly capacities: design review 40 orders, printing 25 orders, cutting 35 orders, and packing 50 orders. The shop receives 30 orders an hour at peak.
steps: Throughput equals the smallest capacity: 25 orders an hour, set by printing.
At 30 orders arriving and 25 printed, a queue grows by 5 orders an hour, so customers wait longer through the peak.
Adding a second printer that brings printing to 45 orders an hour moves the bottleneck to cutting at 35, which now covers the 30-order demand.
example.solution: Invest in printing first. A faster packing station would not raise output at all. After the fix, monitor cutting, the new limiting step, and check whether the printer's cost is covered by the extra orders.

sections.heading: Build and read a department budget
paragraphs: An operating budget plans revenue and expenses for a period. A capital budget plans large purchases of long-term assets. Budget variances compare actual results with the budget. A flexible budget adjusts expected costs to the actual activity level, which gives a fairer comparison than the original static budget.

Department budgets connect to the statements. Operating expenses appear on the income statement. A new machine appears on the balance sheet as an asset and in investing activities on the cash flow statement, and only its depreciation hits the income statement.
bullets: Investigate large variances, not every small one. Here wages are over by 7.5%. Check whether overtime rose because ticket volume grew.
The training savings may be a warning sign: cutting training can raise errors and future costs.

sections.heading: Work a full management case
paragraphs: Management cases ask you to diagnose a problem and defend a plan. Use the functions of management as a checklist: planning (goals and strategy), organizing (structure and resources), staffing (hiring and training), directing or leading (motivation and communication), and controlling (measuring and correcting). Controls can be feedforward (preventing problems before work starts), concurrent (checking during work), or feedback (reviewing results). A balanced scorecard measures success in four areas: financial, customer, internal process, and learning and growth.

practice.task: A regional bakery chain's newest store has 20% lower sales than the others, more customer complaints about wait times, and high staff turnover. Using the management functions, diagnose the problem and propose a plan with two measures of success.
practice.answer: A strong answer gathers evidence first: compare staffing levels, training records, and wait times by hour with other stores. Planning: set a goal such as cutting peak wait time to under 4 minutes within 90 days. Organizing: add a second register during peak hours and move prep work to slower periods. Staffing: use the chain's training program and assign a mentor from a strong store. Leading: hold short daily check-ins and recognize improvements. Controlling: track average wait time and staff turnover weekly, with sales per labor hour as a financial check. It should mention ethics, such as fair scheduling, and the cost of the changes.

terms.definition: The slowest step in a process, which limits total output.
A quality method that uses data to reduce variation and defects.
Know-how gained from experience that is hard to write down.
A budget adjusted to the actual level of activity.
A performance system measuring financial, customer, process, and learning goals.

questions.prompt: Steps in a process can handle 60, 45, and 80 units an hour. Throughput is:
questions.explanation: The slowest step, 45 units, limits output.

questions.prompt: Which step comes first in Lewin's change model?
questions.explanation: Lewin's model is unfreeze, change, refreeze.

questions.prompt: DMAIC is associated with:
questions.explanation: Define, measure, analyze, improve, control is the Six Sigma cycle.

questions.prompt: Buying a $40,000 machine affects the income statement through:
questions.explanation: The machine is an asset; its cost is expensed gradually as depreciation.

questions.prompt: Inspecting materials before production starts is a:
questions.explanation: Feedforward controls prevent problems before work begins.

modules.title: Entrepreneurship: discovery, resources, and daily operations
modules.summary: Find and screen opportunities with evidence, compare funding sources, decide what to hire or outsource, meet legal requirements, and set up operating systems.

sections.heading: Discover and screen opportunities
paragraphs: Opportunities come from problems people already pay to solve, changes in technology or regulation, shifts in demographics and habits, and gaps that competitors ignore. Generate many ideas before judging any. Tools include listing daily frustrations, studying trends in Census and industry data, and the SCAMPER prompts: substitute, combine, adapt, modify, put to another use, eliminate, and reverse.

Screen ideas with weighted criteria. Score each idea on market size, customer urgency, the founder's skills, startup cost, and competition, multiply each score by its weight, and compare totals. Global opportunities follow the same screening plus questions about trade rules, culture, and currency.

sections.heading: Test with customer evidence and decide
paragraphs: Before spending heavily, test the riskiest assumption. Interview potential customers about past behavior, not hypothetical opinions: "When did your bike last break, and what did you do?" is better than "Would you use a repair van?" Run a small test such as a landing page with a sign-up form, a pre-sale, or a minimum viable product (MVP), the simplest version that delivers the core value.

Set a decision rule before testing. For example: proceed if at least 15 of 50 contacted cyclists book a paid repair within two weeks. Stop or change direction (pivot) if not. A decision to stop is a useful result when it saves money.

sections.heading: Fund the venture

rows: Small amounts; put terms in writing
Repayment with interest; often collateral and a personal guarantee
Businesses with cash flow or assets
Small businesses that do not qualify for conventional loans
Time to apply; restrictions on use
Consumer products with a clear story
Significant equity, board seats, pressure for fast growth
Businesses that can grow very large

example.scenario: An angel invests $200,000 for 20% of a startup. What are the valuations?
example.solution: Post-money valuation is 200,000 / 0.20 = $1,000,000. Pre-money valuation is 1,000,000 - 200,000 = $800,000. The founders' share falls from 100% to 80%.

bullets: List startup costs in two groups: one-time costs (equipment, licenses, deposits, initial inventory) and monthly operating costs. Add a reserve, often three to six months of operating costs, because revenue usually starts slower than planned.

Hire an employee when the work is ongoing, central to the business, and needs your direction. Use a contractor or outside firm for specialized or occasional work such as legal filings, bookkeeping, or a logo. Compare the full cost: an employee also brings payroll taxes, insurance, and management time.
paragraphs: Match the funding source to the business. A venture that will grow slowly and steadily rarely fits venture capital, and a business with no cash flow yet rarely qualifies for a bank loan. Compare what each source asks in return.

sections.heading: Legal, tax, and protection setup
steps: Choose a legal structure and register the business name with the state. In Maryland, businesses register with the State Department of Assessments and Taxation.
Get an Employer Identification Number (EIN) from the IRS if you will have employees or form a partnership or corporation.
Obtain required local and state licenses and permits, and check zoning before signing a lease.
Register to collect sales tax if you sell taxable goods or services.
Buy appropriate insurance, such as general liability.
Protect intellectual property: search before choosing a name, register trademarks, and use confidentiality agreements.
Open a separate business bank account and choose accounting software.
paragraphs: Complete the legal setup before the first sale. The steps below are typical for a small Maryland business; confirm each requirement with the state and county, since rules depend on the business type and location.

sections.heading: Design daily operations
paragraphs: Standard operating procedures (SOPs) are written steps for recurring work, so quality does not depend on who is working. Map how an order moves from the customer to delivery, assign an owner to each step, and choose simple systems for scheduling, payments, inventory, and customer records.
Measure productivity with a few numbers, such as jobs completed per day or average time per job. Make risk decisions with the same logic as any business: avoid, reduce, retain, or transfer each risk.

practice.task: For the bike repair van, write a five-step SOP for a repair visit and name one productivity measure and one risk with its treatment.
practice.answer: Sample SOP: (1) Confirm the booking and the problem by text the day before. (2) Arrive, inspect the bike, and give a written estimate before work starts. (3) Complete the repair using the parts checklist. (4) Test-ride or test the repair with the customer and take payment through the card reader. (5) Log the job, parts used, and time in the scheduling app and send a follow-up message. Productivity measure: completed repairs per working day. Risk: injury or damage claims, reduced by a safety checklist and transferred through general liability insurance.

terms.definition: The simplest version of a product that delivers its core value and allows learning from real customers.
A significant change in a business idea based on evidence.
Starting and growing a business with personal funds and revenue.
A company's value immediately after an investment.
Written steps for performing recurring work consistently.
