questions.explanation: The default limit is two speeches per member per question per day.

modules.title: Motion reference: the 13 ranking motions, incidental motions, and voting
modules.summary: A complete table of ranking motions with their rules, incidental motions and motions that bring a question back, vote calculations, nominations and elections, and committee and officer rules.

sections.heading: The 13 ranking motions
paragraphs: The main motion is the lowest-ranking motion. Seven subsidiary motions help dispose of a main motion, and five privileged motions deal with urgent matters unrelated to the pending business. A higher-ranking motion can be made while a lower one is pending, and it is voted on first. The table runs from highest rank (1) to lowest (13). These are the standard rules under Robert's Rules of Order Newly Revised; the full rules include exceptions and conditions.

rows: Fix the time to which to adjourn
Call for the orders of the day
Chair enforces on one member's demand; two-thirds to set aside
Limit or extend limits of debate
Postpone to a certain time (postpone definitely)
If the motion being amended is debatable
Yes (a primary amendment can be amended once)
Yes, and opens the main question to debate

bullets: A memory aid: motions that limit members' rights (previous question, limit debate, suspend the rules) need two-thirds.
Lay on the table is only for setting business aside temporarily for something urgent. Using it to kill a motion is improper; postpone indefinitely is the motion for avoiding a vote.

sections.heading: Incidental motions and motions that bring a question back

rows: Call attention to a rule violation
No second; not debatable; chair rules; made promptly when the error occurs
Second; usually debatable; a majority or tie sustains the chair
Do something the rules otherwise prevent
Second; not debatable; usually two-thirds; cannot suspend bylaws
Prevent an unwanted main motion from being discussed
No second; not debatable; made before debate; two-thirds against consideration sustains it
Split a motion with separate parts
Demand a rising vote when a voice vote seems unclear
No second; one member can demand it
No second; chair or speaker answers
Resume business laid on the table
Vote again on a question decided at the same session
Made only by a member who voted on the prevailing side; debatable if the original motion was; majority
Rescind or amend something previously adopted
Cancel or change an earlier decision
Second; debatable; two-thirds, or majority with previous notice, or majority of the entire membership
Take a referred matter back from a committee

paragraphs: When several motions are pending, vote on the immediately pending one first, then work down. For example, if a main motion, an amendment, and a motion to refer are pending, vote first on referring. If referral fails, vote on the amendment, then on the main motion as amended or not.

sections.heading: Calculate the vote
paragraphs: A majority vote means more than half of the votes cast, not counting blanks or abstentions. Two-thirds means at least two-thirds of the votes cast. Some rules use a different base, such as a majority of the members present or a majority of the entire membership, so always check the base. A tie fails a majority vote. A plurality, the most votes, elects only when the bylaws allow it.

The chair of a large assembly votes when the vote is by ballot or when their vote would change the result, such as breaking or creating a tie, or reaching or blocking two-thirds. In a small board, the chair may vote like other members. Abstaining is a choice not to vote, and it is not counted as a vote.

example.scenario: A chapter has 60 members. Forty attend. On a motion, 22 vote yes, 14 vote no, and 4 abstain.
steps: Votes cast: 22 + 14 = 36.
Majority of votes cast: more than 18, so 19 needed. The motion passes with 22.
Two-thirds of votes cast: 36 x 2/3 = 24 needed. A two-thirds motion would fail with 22.
Majority of the entire membership: more than 30, so 31 needed. That would fail.
example.solution: The same vote passes or fails depending on the rule. Name the base before you calculate.

sections.heading: Nominations, elections, committees, and boards
paragraphs: Nominations can come from the chair, from the floor (no second needed), from a nominating committee, or by ballot. A nominating committee's report does not prevent floor nominations. Closing nominations requires a two-thirds vote, and reopening them requires a majority. Elections are often by ballot, especially when the bylaws require it, and a candidate needs a majority unless the bylaws allow a plurality. An election takes effect immediately if the candidate is present and does not decline, unless the bylaws set another start date.

Standing committees handle ongoing work and are usually named in the bylaws. Special (ad hoc) committees handle one task and dissolve when they report. A committee of the whole is the entire assembly acting as a committee, used for informal discussion. Committees report and recommend; the assembly decides. A board acts only within the authority the bylaws give it and may meet in executive session when confidentiality is needed. The vice president presides when the president is absent or must leave the chair; the treasurer receives, pays, and reports on funds.

practice.task: A main motion to buy chapter jackets is pending. A member moves to amend by adding "not to exceed $500." Before the amendment is voted on, another member moves to refer the motion to the finance committee. Then a member moves the previous question on the referral. (a) List the pending motions from highest to lowest rank. (b) Which is voted on first, and what vote does it need? (c) If referral passes, what happens to the amendment?
practice.answer: (a) Previous question (on referral), commit/refer, amend, main motion. (b) The previous question first, needing two-thirds. If adopted, the assembly votes immediately on referral by majority. (c) If referral passes, the main motion and its pending amendment go to the committee together.

terms.definition: A high-ranking motion about urgent matters not related to pending business, such as adjourning or recessing.
A motion that helps dispose of a main motion, such as amend or refer.
A motion to end debate and vote immediately; requires two-thirds.
A motion, made by a member on the prevailing side, to vote again on a question decided at the same session.
The largest number of votes, which may be less than a majority.

questions.prompt: Which motion has the highest rank?
choices: Fix the time to which to adjourn
questions.explanation: Fix the time to which to adjourn ranks first among the 13.

questions.prompt: Which motion requires a two-thirds vote?
questions.explanation: Closing debate limits members' rights, so it needs two-thirds.

questions.prompt: Who may move to reconsider a vote?
choices: Only a member who voted on the prevailing side
Only the maker of the original motion
questions.explanation: The motion must come from someone who voted with the winning side.

questions.prompt: Thirty votes are cast on a two-thirds motion. The minimum number of yes votes to adopt it is:
questions.explanation: Two-thirds of 30 votes cast is 30 x 2/3 = 20.

questions.prompt: Closing nominations requires:
questions.explanation: Closing nominations limits members' rights, so it needs two-thirds.
